title: Brunelleschi and the Egg
text:
By the early 1400s Florence's cathedral stood unfinished, with a vast octagonal hole where its dome should be. The space was so wide that no one knew how to vault it, since the usual wooden scaffolding to support a dome during construction would have needed more timber than could be found. In 1418 the cathedral authorities held a competition for ideas.

Giorgio Vasari, writing his Lives of the Artists more than a century later, tells how Filippo Brunelleschi handled it. Architects and masters gathered and proposed all sorts of schemes, from columns in the middle to filling the space with earth mixed with coins so that the poor would carry it away afterward. Brunelleschi said he could build the dome without any supporting framework but refused to show his model or explain how, fearing that others would steal the idea.

The others demanded proof. Vasari says Brunelleschi proposed that whoever could make an egg stand upright on a flat marble surface should build the dome, since that would show his ingenuity. Each master tried and failed. Brunelleschi then tapped the egg on the marble, crushing its end, and stood it up. The others protested that they could have done that too. Brunelleschi answered that they would also have known how to vault the dome if they had seen his model.

He received the commission, at first shared with Lorenzo Ghiberti. The dome was completed in 1436 and is still the largest masonry dome in the world.
lesson: An idea explained too early is easy to copy and easy to dismiss. Show what you can do in a way that proves your competence without giving away the method.
source: Giorgio Vasari, Lives of the Most Excellent Painters, Sculptors and Architects, Life of Filippo Brunelleschi
caveat: The egg story is probably apocryphal; a similar tale was later told about Columbus.
